name: Terracotta
lede: Terracotta is the brownish orange of unglazed fired clay, named from the Italian words for baked earth, and as a tube of paint it was a recipe made to match the pot.

sections.title: The clay and the paint
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines terracotta loosely, as any of the many brownish-orange shades of unglazed earthenware [1]. That makes it a range rather than one color, since clay differs from pit to pit and kiln to kiln. A neighbor in the same dictionary, *terra rosa*, is a light red close to [[venetian-red]] [1].

Artists' colormen turned the name into a manufactured paint. The Pigment Compendium reports, on Mayer's authority (1991), that terra cotta was a compound made to imitate clay [2]. Its ingredients were burnt umber, a natural red iron oxide and chalk, in shifting proportions [2]. Baryte, zinc oxide or lithopone could replace the chalk [2]. The paint copied the clay, and the clay lent the name.

The swatch here is a warm, coral-leaning red. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it as a moderate reddish orange, 5.1 units from the center of its block [3]. Its closest names are [[light-coral-red]] (3.4 units away), [[dark-peach]] (4.5), [[dusty-coral]] (4.7) and [[bright-terracotta]] (4.8) [3]. Paterson's range runs browner than this screen color, which is one reason to treat the swatch as a pointer to the clay, not a portrait of it [1].

sections.title: Clay in mosaics and on temple roofs
sections.body:
Gage notes that Greek pebble mosaics gave way, about the third century BC, to regularly cut tesserae, and that a sprinkling of artificially colored terracotta or glass was soon added to the natural stone, widening the range of color [4]. Mosaic materials ranked by worth, with marble at the top, glass next, and stone or terracotta cubes at the bottom; when the dearer kinds ran out, workers sometimes fell back on the cheaper [4].

Fired clay was also painted. A study of a Greek temple's roof terracottas, by Nirmaier in 2000, reports decorative painting in manganese black and hematite red [5]. On the clay soldiers of Xi'an, Bouherour and colleagues identified Han purple in the paint layers [6]. A conservation footnote adds a curiosity: lichen growing on Chinese terracotta soldiers builds calcium oxalate layers, and in laboratory studies copper-bearing pigments such as [[egyptian-blue]] and Han blue and purple inhibited that growth [7].

So the brownish-orange surface in a museum case is often only the base of an object that was once painted.

sections.title: Blue leaves in a terracotta vase
sections.body:
The best-known terracotta in the color books is a painted one. Jan van Huysum's *Flowers in a Terracotta Vase* (1736) hangs in the National Gallery, London [8]. Some of its leaves look blue today, but they were once green: the yellow lake has faded, leaving the blue behind [9].

Ball traces the change in van Huysum's own practice [8]. In a flower piece of 1702 to 1720 the greens contain indigo, while by 1736 he had switched to the new [[prussian-blue]] [8]. The vase gives the picture its title, and the leaves show how a fugitive pigment can rewrite a painting.

Where to look: in an old flower painting, a blue leaf beside a warm orange pot may be a faded green, as in this one [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, a color within four units of this swatch covers at least one per cent of the canvas in 68 paintings, or 0.29 per cent [10]. That is commoner than about half of the named colors [10]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 85 per cent of the 52 paintings the within-painting lens finds, ranked by lightness inside each painting so varnish cannot fake it [10]. It peaks in the 1500s, found in 0.5 per cent of the 2,231 paintings from that century, about twice the baseline rate of the same museums [10]. By country it stands out in India, at 3.4 times the expected rate (14 of 721 paintings) [10].

A stricter lens, within six units and at least five per cent of the canvas, finds 28 paintings [11]. The largest cover is not a pot but a dog: [[painting:rijks-20027480|Portrait of a Puppy]] (1850) by Guillaume Anne van der Brugghen, at 42 per cent, followed by [[painter:john-singer-sargent|Sargent]]'s [[painting:commons-Q20169820|Gitana]] (1876) at 29 per cent [11]. Three of the 97 Rajput paintings in the archive qualify, a rate about 26 times the baseline [11].

The earliest hit is dated 1236 (cma-153618), 585 years before the name's earliest record in our library (1821, Werner as edited by Syme) [10][3]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of any pigment [10]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors.

In Google Books the word *terracotta* climbs from about 2 per cent of its peak level in 1800 to 96 per cent in 2000, with the peak itself in 2002 [12]. Our fashion data lists Terracotta as a named color of both the 2010s and the 2020s [13].

origin.named_after: unglazed fired clay (Italian terra cotta, baked earth)

questions.q: Why do some leaves in van Huysum's Flowers in a Terracotta Vase look blue today?
choices: The yellow lake in the green faded, leaving the blue
He painted them blue on purpose
The terracotta vase reflects blue light
questions.answer: The yellow lake in the green faded, leaving the blue

questions.q: What was artists' terra cotta paint, according to Mayer (1991)?
choices: A mixture of burnt umber, red iron oxide and chalk
Ground fired clay from tile kilns
questions.answer: A mixture of burnt umber, red iron oxide and chalk

questions.q: True or false: terracotta names one fixed color.

openers: The paint called terra cotta was made to imitate the clay, not the other way round.
In van Huysum's flower painting, the blue leaves beside the orange pot were once green.
In our archive the biggest patch of terracotta is a Dutch portrait of a puppy, at 42 per cent of the canvas.

issues: Ball says 'patchy blue leaves', not all: softened
'usually a faded green' overstated: narrowed to this painting
